title: Checkpoint: Growing and Changing
objective: After this level you can explain how genes, hormones and time shape a body from birth to old age.
summary: One life, from zygote to senescent cells. And epigenetics: chemical tags that switch genes on or off without changing DNA, which is why identical twins drift apart as they age.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale: identical twins start the same and drift apart.
cards.body: Identical twins share the same DNA from their first cell. Yet as they age they grow more different, in ways that go deeper than fingerprints. First, one life at a glance. Then, the switches that time flips.

cards.headline: One life, from a single cell

events.label: Egg and sperm (23 chromosomes each) make a zygote with 46
The embryo is now a fetus; birth at about 40 weeks
Hypothalamus to pituitary to ovaries or testes: puberty begins
Telomeres shorten and senescent cells build up

cards.headline: Switches on the DNA
cards.body: Your DNA letters stay the same for life, but your cells attach chemical tags to DNA that turn genes on or off. That's epigenetics. A common tag is a methyl group: when methyl groups sit on a gene, that gene is switched off. Diet and pollutants can change the tags, and cells keep them when they divide. Same text, different highlights.

cards.fact: Identical twins drift apart with age.
cards.context: A 2005 study found that young identical twins have nearly indistinguishable epigenetic tags, while older identical twins differ markedly. Add Level 83's fingerprints, shaped in the womb, and the lesson is clear: genes write the book, but life keeps editing the highlights.

mascot.line: Same genes, different lives, different switches. That's the whole chapter in one pair of twins.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 complete
learned: How one cell, with chromosomes from each parent, grows and specializes into a whole baby.
Why siblings differ though they share parents, and why most traits involve many genes.
What starts puberty: a hormone relay from brain to gland to body, with the brain maturing last.
Why cells age as telomeres shorten, and how epigenetic tags make identical twins drift apart.

questions.prompt: Growing and Changing recap: what do epigenetic tags do?

options.label: Rewrite the letters of your DNA
options.rationale: The DNA sequence stays the same.

options.label: Switch genes on or off without changing the DNA
Add new chromosomes as you age
Shorten telomeres at each division
options.rationale: That's the Hayflick story from Level 85.

questions.explanation: Epigenetic tags, like methyl groups, turn genes on or off without changing the DNA sequence.

questions.prompt: Growing and Changing recap: identical twins share the same DNA. Why do older twins differ more than young ones?

options.label: They lose chromosomes as they age
One twin's DNA letters mutate into the other's
options.rationale: The DNA sequence isn't the difference.

options.label: Identical twins only share DNA as babies
Their epigenetic tags drift apart over time

questions.explanation: Young identical twins have nearly the same epigenetic tags, but older twins differ markedly.

On the day of fertilization

At the start of puberty

questions.explanation: At the end of week 10 of pregnancy, about 8 weeks after fertilization, the embryo is called a fetus.

questions.prompt: Growing and Changing recap, from Level 85: what happens to a chromosome's telomere each time the cell divides?

options.label: It doubles in length
It moves to the middle
options.rationale: It stays at the chromosome's end.

options.label: Some of its repeats are cut off
It becomes an epigenetic tag
options.rationale: Telomeres are repeated DNA, not tags.

questions.explanation: Every division cuts off some telomere repeats, until the cell can no longer divide successfully.

questions.prompt: Growing and Changing recap: identical twins differ in fingerprints and, later, in epigenetic tags. What does that show?

options.label: Identical twins have different DNA
Environment and time shape a body alongside genes
Fingerprints are inherited from grandparents
Epigenetic tags are fixed at birth

questions.explanation: Same DNA, yet womb conditions shape fingerprints and life shapes epigenetic tags: genes aren't the whole story.
